summary.text: A giant planet is a type of planet much larger than Earth, usually made mostly of low-boiling-point materials rather than rock.
The Solar System has four: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, and Jupiter and Saturn are principally hydrogen and helium.
Uranus and Neptune consist of water, ammonia and methane, so many astronomers call them ice giants rather than gas giants.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a giant planet
paragraphs.text: A giant planet is a planet far bigger than Earth, usually built mostly from volatiles, substances that boil at low temperatures, rather than from rock. Our Solar System has four of them: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Many more have been found beyond it. Another name for the group is Jovian planets, from Jove, a second name for the Roman god Jupiter; the label was meant to say that all of them resemble Jupiter.

paragraphs.heading: Gas giants and ice giants
paragraphs.text: The four are not built alike. Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, while Uranus and Neptune are mostly water, ammonia and methane. Because of that difference, many astronomers now keep the label gas giant for Jupiter and Saturn alone and call Uranus and Neptune ice giants, after the ices that dominate their insides. In planet science, ice does not mean frozen solid: water, methane and ammonia are simply grouped as ices, just as hydrogen and helium are grouped as gas and silicates and metals as rock, whatever state they are in.

paragraphs.heading: Not really gas at all
paragraphs.text: The name gas giant was coined in 1952 by the science fiction writer James Blish, and at first it covered all the giant planets. Arguably, it is a poor fit. Through most of the inside of these planets the pressure is so great that matter is not a gas; below the upper atmosphere it is probably past its critical point, a state where liquid and gas can no longer be told apart. A more accurate name would be fluid planet. Even the part we can see is thin: the visible atmosphere reaches perhaps one percent of the way down to the center.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a gas giant
paragraphs.text: Gas giants such as Jupiter and Saturn are thought to have three layers. On the outside is molecular hydrogen; beneath it lies a layer of liquid metallic hydrogen, and at the center there is probably a molten core of rocky material. The metallic layer is the largest part of each planet, and it earns its name because the enormous pressure turns hydrogen into a conductor of electricity. The core is thought to hold heavier elements so hot, around 20,000 K, and under such pressure that how they behave is poorly understood. Heavier elements make up between 3 and 13 percent of the mass of Jupiter and Saturn.

paragraphs.heading: Where the surface should be
paragraphs.text: Giant planets are often described as lacking a solid surface, but it is closer to the truth to say they have no surface at all. Their gases just grow thinner the farther you go from the center, until they cannot be told apart from the interplanetary medium, the matter spread through the space between planets. Whether anything could land on one depends on how big its core is and what it is made of. Jupiter and Saturn still show a face: the outer part of their hydrogen atmosphere holds many layers of visible clouds, mostly water and ammonia.

paragraphs.heading: Giants around other stars
paragraphs.text: Among exoplanets, planets outside the Solar System, the easiest to detect are giants orbiting very close to their stars. They are called hot Jupiters and hot Neptunes because their surfaces are extremely hot. Until telescopes went into space, hot Jupiters were the most common kind of exoplanet known, since instruments on the ground could find them with relative ease.

paragraphs.heading: Where planets end and stars begin
paragraphs.text: Push the mass higher and you reach brown dwarfs, objects big enough to start fusing deuterium, which sit between the largest giant planets and the smallest stars. Exactly where a heavy gas giant ends and a light brown dwarf begins is still debated. The usual dividing line, about 13 times the mass of Jupiter, is a rule of thumb rather than a sharp physical boundary.
